subtopic: INVESTIGATIONS INTO ALLEGED HARMFUL DRUGS
INVESTIGATIONS INTO ALLEGED HARMFUL DRUGS
speechtext:
1.	What are the investigative procedures carried out by the food and drug directorate re drugs suspected of having harmful effects?
2.	In the steps the directorate takes in these matters (a) who initiates the investigation (b) who carries it out (c) how is it assessed, and by whom?
3.	Does the government maintain any liaison with similar food and drug directorates in other countries and, if not, would the government consider setting up liaison?

subtopic: INVESTIGATIONS INTO ALLEGED HARMFUL DRUGS
speechtext:
1. The investigative procedures used by the food and drug directorate regarding drugs suspected of having harmful effects depend on the nature, extent and source of the report received on the harmful effects of the drugs. It is the practice to refer

such reports first to a member of the professional staff of the directorate with knowledge and experience in the drug field on the harmful effects reported. This in turn may lead to a search of the scientific literature, inquiries from or consultation with scientists in the government, in other countries, in pharmaceutical firms, or in scientific organizations.
Where the reports indicate the necessity for inspecting the facilities of the pharmaceutical manufacturer, this is carried out by the inspection services of the directorate. Where laboratory studies are indicated the problem is referred to the laboratory services of the directorate for investigation.
2.	The investigations are initiated under the authority of the director and are assigned to members of the professional staff of the food and drug directorate considered to have the necessary knowledge, skills and experience to study the problem. The results of the investigations are assessed by the professional staff in consultation with the director or referred to an advisory panel on drugs.
3.	There are frequent conversations and interchange of information respecting problems in the drug field between the technical staff of the food and drug directorate and the food and drug administration in the United States, the ministry of health in the United Kingdom and in Australia, and similar government agencies in other countries.
Liaison is also maintained with the groups in the world health organization concerned with the international pharmacopoeia and the biological standardization of drugs, and the food and drug directorate is represented on panels and committees of organizations concerned with the establishment of official compendia on drugs in the United Kingdom and the United States.
In his statement to the House of Commons on October 26 the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that the Canadian delegation to the world health assembly held last May initiated and co-sponsored a special resolution designed to promote greater international co-operation in the drug field and particularly to secure regular exchange of information on the safety and efficacy of pharmaceutical preparations. The international type of liaison envisaged in the resolution is considered a very effective method of dealing with the subject.

speechtext:
1.	What contributions did the federal government make to initiate spruce budworm control operations in eastern Canada?
2.	Have the control operations yielded substantial benefits?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of Forestry
subtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM CONTROL
speechtext:
During the entire period of the budworm outbreak, which started about 1949, officers of the Department of Forestry have carried out surveys to delineate areas of high hazard, where
Questions
control operations would be needed to prevent serious timber mortality. They also carried out intensive biological studies and provided technical advisory services to the provincial governments of New Brunswick and Quebec, and to forest industrial associations in the two provinces.
The federal government paid one third of the cost of control operations in New Brunswick since 1953. Over the past ten years the federal government paid approximately $3.8 million to the cost of the control program.
The spraying operations prevented serious timber mortality throughout the huge infestation area. Without this direct intervention severe timber mortality would have occurred over an area of at least four or five million acres, and a fire hazard of extreme proportions would have been created.

subtopic: FEDERAL JURISDICTION OVER SALMON SPAWNING STREAMS
FEDERAL JURISDICTION OVER SALMON SPAWNING STREAMS
speechtext:
1.	What authority does the Department of Fisheries have to deal with companies or persons whose logging operations result in salmon spawning streams being clogged with debris, and has this authority been exercised in the Queen Charlotte islands at any time during the past ten years and, if so, what action was taken, against whom, at what time, for what reason, and what resulted therefrom?
2.	What authority does the Department of Fisheries have to deal with companies or persons who remove gravel from salmon spawning streams and has this authority been exercised on the Queen Charlotte islands at any time during the past ten years and, if so, what action has been taken against whom, at what time, for what reason, and what resulted therefrom?

subtopic: FEDERAL JURISDICTION OVER SALMON SPAWNING STREAMS
speechtext:
1. Section 33, subsection 3, of the Fisheries Act, which reads as follows:
(3) No such person engaging in logging, lumbering, land clearing or other operations, shall put or knowingly permit to be put, any slash, stumps

or other debris into any water frequented by fish or that flows into such water, or on the ice over either such water, or at a place from which it is likely to be carried into either such water.
Departmental policy is to advise offenders of this authority and the penalties provided, with a request for co-operation, which is normally forthcoming. In the past ten years no prosecutions have been necessary on Queen Charlotte islands, although numerous warnings were given, amongst which were removal of debris from Dana inlet creek in 1959, Copper river, Hannat creek and Terundle creek in 1962, all followed by observance of the provisions of the act.
2. Section 30 of the Fisheries Act provides that the eggs or fry of fish on the spawning grounds shall not at any time be destroyed.
The problem has been dealt with by asking companies or persons to limit operations to other areas or to times when eggs and fry are not present. The department is aware that in free periods gravel is stockpiled, as on the Mammon river. This has an undesirable effect and accordingly other means, such as use of dry backwaters, are suggested. In some areas adjustment is easy, for example on the Deena river the company involved was persuaded to use gravel from the intertidal zone.
In recognition of the possibility of serious effects on the Yakoun, one of the largest rivers, and now being considered for logging development, the co-operation of the company and the British Columbia forest service is being enlisted to avoid overremoval.

speechtext:

subtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM OUTBREAK, EASTERN CANADA
SPRUCE BUDWORM OUTBREAK, EASTERN CANADA
speechtext: What is the present status of the spruce budworm outbreak in eastern Canada and, will chemical control operations be necessary in 1963?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of Forestry
subtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM OUTBREAK, EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
The outbreak is no longer active in northern New Brunswick and the adjacent part of Quebec. Consequently no control operations will be necessary in these areas in 1963.
In central New Brunswick, budworm populations remain at hazardous levels in about one dozen localities, aggregating some 360,000 acres. This is the smallest acreage of hazard-
ous infestation that has been experienced since 1952. Spraying operations should be carried out in 1963 to reduce the budworm population on these 360,000 acres. No other aerial spraying operations against the budworm are anticipated in eastern Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the motion for second reading of the bill to provide for the establishment of an Atlantic development board I wish only to thank hon. members from all quarters in the house for the interest they have all taken in the bill and the comments that have been made, some of which were constructive in character.
I do not believe that any points have been raised to which I at this moment wish to make reference, although I believe some observations have been made which would lead to a somewhat detailed discussion of a somewhat political nature if I were inclined to do so. I do feel that the subject and the possibilities of this board are sufficiently important and sufficiently extensive that, without any particular loss to this house so far as information is concerned, I might just pass them by.
The principle of the bill now before us for second reading is well known. The comments that have been made in the house in connection with the special situation of the Atlantic provinces are likewise, I believe, of general acceptance. My opinion is that we are asked by the motion to approve the principle and I doubt that there is very much objection to such approval of the principle.
I do not think that we in the maritimes should emphasize the disabilities with regard to which we may be having some difficulty in an economic sense. It has always been my opinion that we who are fortunate enough
[Miss LaMarsh.l
to have been born and lived in those provinces down by the sea should emphasize the advantages we have rather than emphasizing to an undue degree the disabilities of living in a fringe area of a great nation. I think we can do much better for ourselves if we adopt such an attitude, always keeping in mind, however, that the special privileges and rights inherent in all agreements made previously with the central government should be brought to the attention of the central gov-* ernment from time to time.
Yesterday the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) put on record certain specific questions which he asked me to answer.
I am quite prepared to answer them but I venture the observation that this would lead to nothing except a discussion of a political nature in which he and his party would come off second best. That is my feeling. Therefore, with that in mind I do not propose to remind him of certain things. He has been a member of the house since 1953. He is a veteran of the house. I do not know how much pressure he brought to bear on the government of which he was a supporter when they were in office. I do know something of the results that were achieved, and those results were practically nil. I will give him full marks for his effort but I am sure he will have to acknowledge that the efforts of the government which he supported and which held office prior to the present administration were not productive of results to any great degree.
I know that some members will say: Oh, yes, but we had the equalization grants, and so on. I emphasize that the real principle which we are debating at the present time and in regard to which I am offering these comments is that there shall be a board established with certain duties devolving upon it. Those duties, I submit, and I am sure those who have read the bill will agree, are of a very broad and flexible nature, and so they should be. Some hon. members have suggested, and I believe that to a certain degree at least this was recommended by the commission on Canada's economic prospects, that a board or commission should be established and a certain fixed amount of public funds should be placed in their hands for disposal, but to me that is an abrogation of the principle of responsibility. I do not feel that any parliament should delegate powers of that nature.
But what are we doing under this legislation? We are providing the machinery by which an examination may be made of any promising situation existing in the Atlantic provinces. That is exactly what we have not had up until now. No one knows better than some members of this house the many trips to Ottawa made by representatives of each of

the provinces in the eastern part of Canada for many years now for the specific purpose of bringing certain things to the attention of the authorities. In that regard I would say that generally speaking, regardless of the political complexion of the government which has brought these matters to the attention of the central government, they have all had a degree of merit and have deserved consideration.
But after you get through the maze of departmental activity in Ottawa and finally find the proper department, you possibly run into a situation that again presents a difficulty not easily to be surmounted. This all adds up to a tremendous loss of time and the greatest of difficulty. Then these representatives return to their respective provinces and become engrossed in their day to day duty. I am speaking of men in public life now.

My answer to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is definitely in the negative, and I will try to explain to the satisfaction of my hon. friend and the house why I say this. In my view there are many promising situations, some of which I skipped over quite lightly yesterday. If a board is set up as envisaged by this legislation and if that board has certain fixed duties and responsibilities, even though they are flexible and even though they are broad, there will be some assurance that if proposals have been proven to be economically sound after investigation and are finally put before the central government, as I would hope some such proposals would be, they will have received a thorough examination and the department concerned or the government or cabinet, call it what you will, will be confident that they have had a certain degree of examination and will be prepared to deal with them in a minimum of time. That is the reason why I answered categorically and quickly to the question asked by my hon. friend, who I know is interested in the maritimes and has not asked the question to embarrass me or anyone else.
Now, Mr. Speaker, referring again to the matter of investigation, I may say it is envisaged that this body shall have authority to engage the services of experts in certain
Atlantic Development Board fields who may be available in Ottawa in the various departments, and there are many of them, or this body may employ consultants and engage anyone they think has specialized knowledge concerning the particular matter under investigation. I am very certain that the fact they have that kind of power delegated to them is going to place them in a position where they will be able to act quickly, and with a minimum loss of time investigate any promising situation which, after careful examination, they feel is deserving of consideration.
Within the last 24 hours, I have received quite a few telephone calls. May I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that they have come from every one of the Atlantic provinces. These people did not call for the purpose of saying what a great thing the Atlantic development board act would be. Generally speaking, they said, when do we get the board established and when will we be able to bring to the board's attention these promising situations? In my opinion, this was a very healthy sign signifying the ultimate success of this board.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the motion is that the bill receive second reading. I do not believe there is much more I can say at the moment that would be very illuminating. The principle of the bill is involved here and I believe all members of this house are in favour of the principle. I do not think there is any question about that. However, I would not say that there might not be the odd section that might not be capable of amendment because I think that it takes the combined knowledge of everyone to think of everything. I am rather of the opinion, therefore, that there may be some sections that we might properly consider amending slightly. As a matter of fact, I have one such amendment in mind at the moment.
Since we are talking about the principle, and since we are talking about the general idea that we want to do something, I wonder if it would not be a good idea to forget everything that has happened prior to 1962 or even prior to December 5, 1962. Let us go forward with this bill. Let us consider it in the light of the possibilities that may be embodied in the bill, the things that it may accomplish. If we devote our time to finding fault with the bill and finding fault with each other or engaging in a political hassle, which is not uncommon in the maritimes and other parts of Canada, then I have no doubt that we might consider the activities and results of this board may not amount to a great deal. If we make up our minds that we are not going to worry about who gets the credit for it but we are going to go ahead to ensure that this board will be able to investigate situations and finally come up with solutions

Atlantic Development Board which may be of benefit to our part of Canada, then that will be a good thing to do and will produce beneficial results.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think that is all I have to say on second reading. I would hope the house would agree unanimously on the principle. I think all hon. members do. Then, we can go into committee and discuss the various sections of the bill itself. It would be my hope that discussion might be expedited as much as possible, with due regard for the rights of every member to express his opinion, to express his interest and to suggest improvements, as long as those suggestions are based on the general idea of wanting to be helpful and not obstructive. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

I would remind the minister that in the period from 1953 to 1957 a number of very great works were carried on in the Atlantic provinces. I do not think any better decision was ever made by the Department of National Defence than the decision to put camp Gagetown in New Brunswick. I know something about why that decision was made. There were many other places where, from a military standpoint, it might just as well have been put, but it was placed there because it was known it would help the economy of that province and it has, to a marked degree, as anybody who visits the city of Fredericton or the city of Saint John knows. I predict that in time it will be one of the great monuments to the wisdom of the Canadian people in developing all parts of their country.
I am going to say something now which, no doubt, will be surprising to hon. members opposite. I think it is unfortunate that the government to which I belonged, the former Liberal government, and Liberal governments before that did not, in the field of defence production, do the same as they did with respect to camp Gagetown, by developing production facilities in the Atlantic provinces. I think, looking back on it, we could have done better for our country than we did, had we done that. Now, sir, I want to make one observation, and one only, about the debate on this bill. On behalf of the Liberal opposition I am authorized to say that we are prepared, in order to expedite the enactment of this legislation and also of a number of other measures which are on the order paper, to be satisfied with having two speakers from our party on second reading of this bill-and I make this offer specifically with respect to this billon the understanding that the excellent suggestion made by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) the other day will be carried out by the government, and that this bill will be sent to a standing committee. I would suppose that the appropriate committee would be the banking and commerce committee, but it could be sent to whatever committee the government wishes. There it could be carefully examined and the officials could tell us what is going to happen after this board is set up.
I quite agree with the minister that that is really what is important. Merely enacting this measure and having a board is not going to get us very far. It is particularly important in relation to the other legislation, which has suggested in the minds of many hon. members that there may be a good deal of overlapping and duplication between these various agencies which the government is proposing and some of the agencies which have already been set up.
So, sir, I say that we are prepared to have only two speakers on second reading of this bill, on the understanding, of course, that the government supporters do not put up more than two speakers, and on the understanding

Atlantic Development Board that the bill is not brought here in committee of the whole until it has first had careful examination by a standing committee. Then, of course, it will come to the committee of the whole where any hon. member who wishes to deal with the clauses can do so. However, I feel that a measure as important as the minister has told us this one is going to be, certainly ought to have the kind of careful examination that really is not possible in committee of the whole in this house, particularly at a time when there seems to be a general disposition in the house to try and speed up legislation. It is with a view to assisting the minister and the government in getting this measure enacted expeditiously, and in getting the best possible measure enacted, that I make this suggestion. Perhaps the minister can indicate in due course what view the government takes of that suggestion.
Now I come to the bill itself, and I must say that I read it with the greatest disappointment. I think that all those in the Atlantic provinces who read this bill and who understand its purport will also be very much disappointed. I say that because this bill does not do what I think all of us had been led by the speech from the throne and the program of the government before June 18 to feel the government intended to do in this matter. To put it bluntly, sir, we expected an executive agency, and all this is is another advisory body. I say that is not good enough.
Before anyone asks me: "Are you going to oppose the bill?", I am going to say this. I am going to say that I was brought up on the principle that nothing in this world is perfect, that the perfectionist generally gets nothing, and that half a loaf is better than no bread. I do not think that this bill is even half the loaf which was promised: I think it is only a crust. But I think it would be foolish to reject even the crust, and for my part I would certainly not join in rejecting it on second reading. It might well be that when we get into committee and have a chance to consider the matter, it would be found, as the minister has said, that this bill is not regarded by the government as perfect and we could make some improvements in it. I do not think it would ever be acceptable, but it would make it more useful than it would now seem to me to be.
Now, sir, if one may judge from what one has read about it in advance in the press, it would seem that the bill is more or less the product of a mutual back scratching match between the publisher of the Atlantic Advocate and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker), who lavish the most exaggerated amount of praise upon each other,

which in most cases is rather empty of content. But there is another journal in the Atlantic provinces which calls itself an independent newspaper, and which I think is an independent newspaper. Although I do not think anybody would accuse it of being a supporter of the Liberal party, it is a newspaper for which I have very high regard indeed. That newspaper is the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, and on November 19 it had this to say about this very bill:
If the promised Atlantic provinces development board is to be a federal advisory commission (as now appears to be the case), two conditions will have to be met before its effectiveness can be assured.

A policy of making public its recommendations, possibly at the same time that it forwards them to the government, will have to be followed not only to "prove" the board's independence of the governments of the day, but to establish in public opinion its credentials as an effective planning agency.
As I read the bill-the minister may say that I have misinterpreted it-the board is to report only to the minister; it is not to report in any public way at all. This editorial goes on:
2.	To the same end, the policy of appointment to the board will have to be not merely barren of party considerations-
Apparently the Halifax Chronicle-Herald does not realize that the Atlantic provinces have completely run out of defeated government candidates without employment, because it seems to fear that some of them will be appointed to this board, and it is warning in advance, perhaps, that even the colleagues of ex-provincial premiers are people who might be appointed.

DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FEDERAL DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the setting up of a department of federal-provincial affairs under the direction of a full-time minister.
He said: In rising to speak on this resolution, I believe we have before us one of the most important items we could consider relating to the general efficiency of government and the observance of the spirit of confederation which originally brought the provinces together to form this great country of Canada.
One of the most disturbing elements on the Canadian scene is the developing or continuing lack of a national spirit-that spirit which brought Canada into confederation. At a time when we should be strengthening the bonds of confederation it would seem that our governments, through policies of indecision and through the insidious usurpation and infringement of provincial rights, are weakening the province's unity. As our way of life becomes more complicated and
Dominion-Provincial Relations as the development of the country fosters programs which of necessity transcend provincial boundaries it is absolutely essential that the closer co-operative working relationships which are obviously required between the national government and the various provincial governments be as harmonious and correlated as possible.
An example of this is the Columbia river project. This involves the treaty whose negotiation the Liberal government blocked in 1955-a treaty which was formally signed in 1960, just prior to the retirement of President Eisenhower, and which has yet to be ratified. The negotiator and the spokesman for the government at that time was the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton) who was then the minister of justice. I believe the hon. gentleman was more successful as minister of justice than he was as a negotiator with the provincial government. Anyway, I could never quite reconcile how a minister of justice could be concerned in dealing with a hydroelectric development project. Perhaps a redeeming feature of this situation is that through his dabbling in provincial affairs the hon. gentleman has given himself some background for his new prospective role. In my opinion, however, the Columbia river project would have been much further advanced had these negotiations been directed by a government minister whose direct responsibility would be to deal with such matters. This same principle applies to many different types of projects. Among them could be included irrigation projects, a nationl power grid, the national highways program, international highways such as the Alaska highway and the proposed Maritime-Montreal turnpike as well as the question of standardized electoral techniques.
I think that in considering this subject we should revert to the principles that brought us to confederation. Basically, these were founded on an agreement between the provinces which resulted in the formation of our country, Canada. The trend today is to attempt to cure economic ills, not by the use of mechanisms of our constitution but by special and often ineffective federal action. I think one of the reasons we fail to achieve close co-operation and harmony in the working of our government at the provincial and federal levels is simply that we are getting away from the spirit of the British North America Act which specifically defines the responsibilities of the two levels of government. It is my opinion that we are less in need of amendments to the British North America Act than we are of a return to the basic principles which are expressed in it. I feel also with respect to the appointments of the many boards, royal commissions and

Dominion-Provincial Relations special government agencies which now abound in this country and which are being added to by legislation already before this house, that unless we do have in the federal government a special department concerned with the overlapping of what could be conflicting areas of responsibility, we are not going to reach, through those boards and commissions, the objectives upon which we mutually agree.
We have been speaking in this house this afternoon about an Atlantic development board. This is to be a national board and obviously it will have very close relationships with the Atlantic provinces economic council. It will also overlap considerably with the area of responsibility of the national economic development board and of the national productivity council. To avoid confusion and to increase efficiency, a department of government specifically set up with the responsibility of dealing with such questions involving both the dominion and provincial governments would certainly appear to be most desirable.
There are any number of instances which could be quoted of occasions upon which the federal government has been at cross purposes with the provincial governments. We can recall what happened in connection with the Newfoundland loggers strike, the relations between the federal government and the province of Quebec over university grants and even in connection with co-operative programs of hospital finance and the fair allocation of federal government appointments to Quebec citizens. There is also the question of equalizing taxation on private utilities with that imposed on public utilities, a problem which so often relates to provincial governments but one whose correction rests entirely within the hands of the dominion government. I am reminded that just a few weeks ago this matter was discussed here in the house. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) said he could not consider action at that time because he would not want to be interfering with a provincial election. Yet this question of the taxation of utilities which are continuing to operate through private enterprise is a real problem, and one which is not being handled in a satisfactory way by the federal government.
All this makes difficulties for provincial governments. I could go on to cite a number of other cases of this kind but it would simply bring us again to our main point, namely that there are many problems today arising between the two levels of government whose solution could be facilitated if only there were a single federal government department charged with specific responsibility for this field of activity.


There are other fields in which liaison between federal and provincial governments is far from perfect. There is, for example, the question of the allocation of tax fields. This is in itself a very important question and there is a great deal to be done before satisfactory arrangements can be completed. Then there is the question of the uniformity of certain types of legislation arising simply because our country, expanding as it has, faces problems which cut across provincial boundaries. With regard to this, I think the federal government has a certain amount of responsibility, at least to provide for the appropriate liaison and to see that the development of the country as a whole as well as in the provincial areas goes ahead as it should.
Another matter which might be mentioned is the question of electoral procedure in this country, which is far from uniform. This is not an appropriate subject for legislation by the federal government but, certainly, uniformity is something which the federal government could facilitate if there were a closer understanding between provincial and federal governments. There is the problem of social welfare standards. There is the problem of agricultural policies which are at variance with each other simply because we have not reached a stage of correlated integration of policies between the provinces.
I think that in all of these matters if there were a department of government, with a minister, a deputy minister and a proper administrative set-up, certainly many of these problems could be minimized and brought to pass much more efficiently. There is the question of policy relating to the development of our natural resources. We recall the "resources for tomorrow" conference, and I think that anybody who took part in that conference will agree that one of the difficulties which faced the conference was the lack of proper preparation, as well as the lack of proper follow-through on some of the decisions reached. Again, a specific department of government would be able to handle these problems much more effectively than they are handled at present. These are matters which we see, and there are other particular needs for co-operation which will be of more importance in the future. We need very urgently in Canada a definite highway development policy. In connection with that, we need certainly many changes in our transportation policy. These involve the provincial governments as well. These changes apply both to rail and to highway transport, and also to air transport. Here again a much closer co-operation and effective working together is very important at this time.
The trend in Canada today-we have seen this in the house during these past few

Dominion-Provincial Relations
days-is towards federally-appointed boards. Rather than to impose the will of the federal government upon the provinces, as is done very often through these boards, it would be much better and would pay much greater respect to our constitution to bring about a closer spirit of harmony in establishing the necessary machinery to make effective the recommendations of these boards. Our proposal in bringing forward this resolution at this time is that there should be a department of federal-provincial affairs under a full-time minister. His responsibility would be one of co-ordination, of regional orientation, so that we would not have the undignified spectacle we frequently see in Canada of two levels of government, and sometimes three, engaging in mutually contradictory policies, without the fruitful result which we expect through the action taken, while at the same time costing large amounts of taxpayers' money.
There are many examples I could cite to support this argument. In the United States the government, which is a federal government in many respects similar to our own, has its secretary of the interior. Coming to our provincial governments, several of them have already realized the need for this very thing, and both in Manitoba and Ontario- there may be others-there are portfolios of provincial-federal affairs. This leads up to the fact that this need is recognized at the provincial level, and they are looking toward something which will tie the ends together at the federal level.
It is worthy of note that we should look at the friction which often occurs between provincial and federal governments, bearing in mind that many of these problems can be ironed out without the name calling and the buck passing which is associated all too frequently with federal-provincial affairs at this time. I think in this regard of a number of statements which the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton) has made with regard to the development of the British Columbia power issue. Again, I wonder what is the responsibility of a former minister of justice in getting himself involved in this very matter anyway. It lowers his own status, which he should be maintaining as minister of justice, and it involves him in matters which are actually none of his business. In the United States, who is the man responsible for heading up these negotiations? He is the secretary of the interior, and rightfully so because that is his responsibility.
But again, behind all of this I would say that there is the basic issue of democratic government itself in Canada. More and more power assigned to boards means less and less
power to elected representatives, who frequently have responsibilities under the constitution trenching in on the same field. One of the dangers which threatens democratic government in Canada today at any level is where the responsibilities of elected representatives, through the processes of democracy, are assigned to appointed boards and committees. This is not in accordance with my understanding of the basic principles of democracy. It develops the situation, which is becoming all too common in our midst, of bureaucracy at government level, and I think that the second phase of the Glassco commission reports brings this very clearly to our attention. Bureaucracy is the very negation of democracy. It frequently adopts lines of policy which even this house cannot completely keep under control from day to day. An example of this in recent days has been the dispute between the board of broadcast governors and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. My proposal here tonight is a means of giving the provinces a chance to be heard on major policy decisions of the federal government, and even to get action on many matters which are neglected, of which resources and transport policy are two of the most conspicuous. We believe that government closest to the people is the best government, and this proposal is worth 10,000 boards in getting effective government action in accordance with the real wishes of the Canadian people on a hundred matters on which they are dissatisfied at the present time.
In a matter of five years we will be celebrating the centennial of our country. The preparations for this centennial are something which concerns everybody in Canada, as well as government at every level. The experiment which is Canada-the bringing together of people whose background represents two great nations, and adding on top of them many new Canadians of different ethnic backgrounds-is an experiment which, if it should fail, would rock the very foundations of our hopes for peace. If we cannot succeed and cannot bring this aim to a great climax at our one hundredth anniversary, then what hope is there in this world for peace? I am convinced that the experiment which is Canada can be a living proof of what can be done to bring peoples together so as to form a spirit of national unity, which in this case will provide the great strength which potentially is ours in Canada, but which will prove that democratic government is the answer to our governmental needs, even in an age such as we are part of. Therefore I commend to the members of this house that they give very careful consideration to the basic purpose and intent behind this resolution, in the

Dominion-Provincial Relations hope that we could impress upon the government at this time that one of the most positive actions it could take would be to set up such a department of government for the purpose I have just briefly referred to.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few brief words of approval and gratification for the proposal which the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) has put before us. I say gratification because for the last nine years the members of our party have put forward in this house similar measures, and it is very encouraging to us, sir, to find that other parties are now thinking along similar lines.
We endorse the principle the bill establishes. Actually, it would have been surprising that we would not do so as I think the bill is almost non-political. The need for the action proposed is so apparent and the remedy put forward so logical that it would be strange if we found much opposition to the action either in this house or in the country. It is true that in the founding convention of my own party this clause appears in our program:
Immediately following confederation a federal minister was given special responsibility for relations with the provinces. It is time to revive that post. The New Democratic party aims to create a federal-provincial relations department to maintain and extend co-operation with the provinces and to co-ordinate and act as a special secretariat for joint committees and councils.
It is true that appears in a political program. However, it is likely that similar ideas appear in other political programs. As I say, the matter is hardly political. Particularly in this house where we see every day measures which come before us and with which we are asked to deal, I do not think there could be much opposition to the step proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer. When we deal with matters of finance, industry, agriculture, labour or health, it is apparent that these matters go far beyond the constitutional authority which we have under the present arrangements in Canada. We deal here with the results of economics and those economics have no provincial boundaries. The economics of the farm, the factory or the home are at once interprovincial and federal. We cannot separate them and we cannot deal with them properly on a separate basis as we have been trying to do for so long.
It is true that we have in Canada three levels of government, namely federal, provincial and municipal. But actually we have one people. When I say we have three levels of government I should like to suggest to hon. members to consider what seems to me to be almost a fourth level of government which is coming about and I think being made

apparent through the very needs of the constitutional situation. That fourth level of government is the interprovincial one. We now have every year meetings between the leaders of the provincial governments where they come together and discuss joint problems. The reason they do this is that there is no appropriate machinery at the provincial-federal level such as that which is proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer, and which would offer a basis for handling such consultations.
When my grandfather came to this continent, Mr. Speaker, in 1887 it took him two weeks to go across the continent. Today I think I can do it in four hours. In his day it would have taken two weeks for a picture to be taken and transported across the country. Today the same thing can be accomplished in a matter of minutes or seconds. Those two points may illustrate the great changes, economic and social, which have taken place in the country, and which we should also take steps to meet on a constitutional and administrative basis.
I think the proposal to create a federal-provincial ministry with a specific minister to deal with the class of matters in which the federal-provincial relationship is involved is necessary at this time. I hope the matter may be brought to a vote. In order that others may speak, I will not further take up the time of the house, except to urge that the matter be supported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the house, has as its purpose the setting up of a department of federal-provincial affairs under the direction of a full time minister. Many provincial governments have made an approach, through the press and through direct representation to the federal government, to have representation and more say on certain matters emanating from the federal picture which affects them within the provinces. As to whether the setting up of a new department to handle this matter, even though it has only as its limitations the question of co-ordination, is one of the matters which I believe would need to be approached in a very careful manner.
I do not believe that the mover of this resolution had in mind the setting up of a department that would be a fifth wheel. However, in all probability it might grow into just that very thing. In other words, the only person or persons in the federal government who know anything about, for example, health problems are the people who deal with those problems in the health department. If someone else is co-ordinating these matters pertaining to health, they in turn would need to work through the health department if any

intelligence were to be put into the negotiations between federal and provincial people. One could go on down the line and draw a parallel with a vast number of programs which are carried out between the provincial governments and the federal government. In setting up a department in order to bring federal and provincial governments closer together, you might be destroying the present relationship which exists between the department in the federal government taking care of those problems and the department in the provincial government where the similar problems from a provincial point of view are being taken care of. In other words, those two departments have a working relationship. They understand one another. They are in constant communication. Where there are matters that are to be handled by the two governments, it is the people who are concerned in these respective departments that get together and discuss those matters. If you were to set up a minister whose job it would be to look after federal-provincial relationships, unless his duties were thoroughly defined and unless he kept within those limitations there would be, before long, instances in which he would be in the hair of the existing departments handling those matters.
Let us go on to a second question. I wish to speak for a few minutes about the magnitude of the problem as between say the federal and the provincial levels. I should like to spend just a few moments in examining that magnitude as between the federal government and for example the province of Alberta. The federal government contributed to the province of Alberta 44.4 per cent of the money which it spent during the fiscal year 1959-60. Those are the last available figures from the financial statistics of the provincial governments issued by the dominion bureau of statistics.
To go back a step, I should like to point out that the gross revenue of the province of Alberta in 1959-60 was $332,755,000 which included conditional and unconditional grants from the federal government totalling $147,970,000. Unconditional grants amounted to $59,009,000 and conditional grants amounted to $88,961,000. The figure of $147,970,000, which is the sum of the amounts for conditional and unconditional grants, represented 44.4 per cent of the money spent by the government of Alberta during that particular year, and that money came from the federal treasury. To put it another way, well over $1 out of $3 came from the federal government.
It might be well to put figures on the record to show that there has been a tremendous increase in these grants over the past
Dominion-Provincial Relations few years. The contribution of the federal treasury in 1956-57 was $89,685,000 while in 1959-60 it was $147,970,000. In other words, there has been an increase from 1956-57 to 1959-60 of $58,285,000 in the revenue which the province of Alberta has received from the federal government, and that took place since this government came into office.
We are often damned and criticized for deficit financing, but this deficit has come about as a result of the generous conditional and unconditional grants made to the province of Alberta and other provinces. But the figures I have given might well be analysed by all those who have a desire to criticize this government for its generous contributions to support programs administered by the provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, I shall strive to bring the debate back to the level where it was during the speech of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), that is a higher level than during the remarks of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat.
Since confederation, there have been great autonomists, particularly in the province of Quebec. To name only a few, there were Messrs. Honore Mercier, L. A. Taschereau and Duplessis and the present premier, the Hon. Jean Lesage. One can see therefore that only a few years after confederation, there was already some friction between the central government and the provinces. Without those difficulties, we would not have had the great

men who fought against the federal government at that time. It would seem then that provincial rights have been threatened since confederation. On the other hand, confederation would not have been possible if the provinces had not received assurances that their rights would be respected. I remember that, barely two years ago, my chief, the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Pearson), suggested that a department be set up to deal exclusively with federal-provincial affairs.
I recognize that, in some areas, that suggestion was very badly received, whereas it was much better received in others. Some claimed for example that when it came to interpreting the constitution, the Minister of Justice was the one to do so, and that the appointment of another minister would result in duplication of responsibilities. Others said: When we come to Ottawa to secure grants, we go to the Minister of Finance and not to a minister of federal-provincial affairs.
I am convinced that if we had a department of federal-provincial affairs, it could continually discuss the situation with the provincial ministers. Besides, Ontario and Manitoba already have such a ministry; the premier of the province of Quebec said that he was thinking of setting up such a department. In fact, the heads of those departments would report to their respective governments on the discussions they would have together.
Besides, some steps have already been taken to unify opinions in the various provinces. At the call of Premier Jean Lesage, all provincial premiers met three years ago in Quebec to consider their problems in regard to the federal government. Another meeting was held in Charlottetown last year and this year it was in Victoria. This shows that there are continuing problems, problems which have been getting worse particularly since 1931, when the Westminster statute was signed. We have seen the development of these problems since the war because of Canada's expansion and the responsibilities it had accepted toward the outside world. The federal government needed increased revenues, and so did the provinces because of their continued development. But now, both levels of government have seen that it is impossible for each level to tax individually because the population cannot accept further increased taxation. There had to be an agreement between the various provinces and the federal government in order to know definitely in what field one level of government could levy taxes and in what field the other level could do so.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
I admit it is impossible to come to a solution overnight, because there are great difficulties standing in the way.
We know that the Liberal party has developed an equalization plan in order to allow the federal government to give more to the underdeveloped provinces, to those who are in greater need of assistance. In Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, which are immensely rich provinces, that problem does not exist, because their revenue is adequate and they do not seem to have any concern about the poorer provinces.
I think it was the desire of all federal governments to help more particularly those provinces who needed greater assistance. But, in some quarters, there was reluctance to welcome such an arrangement. Consequently, in order to correct the situation, we should set up an agency which would constantly study each problem in the light of its inherent difficulties, which would allow the government to be able to make wise decisions.
Let us take, for instance, the problem of highway transportation. The MacPherson commission suggested that the railways should not enter that field. Highway transportation originated because of a lack of foresight on the part of railway companies; it developed these come under provincial jurisdiction.
The MacPherson commission actually said to the railways: Go ahead and keep away from that. Those are problems that could be discussed between the provincial and federal governments, so that both parties may benefit from it.
There is the matter of the Columbia river that seemed to be settled a long time ago, but which is cropping up again today.
Relations are strained between the federal government and the British Columbia government, regardless of the party in power.
All those matters could be settled if we had a body which would look into those problems regularly and report its findings to the government. The cabinet might be able then to find a way of correcting the situation once and for all, after hearing both parties.
Besides, the government will soon propose the repatriation of the constitution. How are we going to repatriate the constitution if we have had no time to study it and put it in order?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FEDERAL DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), which proposes the setting up of a department of federal-provincial affairs, under the direction of a full-time minister, is of the utmost importance for the good administration of our country, because it aims at eliminating all the problems that arise from the fact that the federal government trespasses on provincial laws and privileges and at restoring justice within the limits set by the Confederation Act of 1867.
The centralization implemented in such a hateful way by the central government at the time of the Liberal administration was a source of continuous friction between the provincial states and the federal state, especially with regard to taxation.
Under the Conservative administration, the situation has remained almost unchanged.
On the other hand, since it was always quite difficult to settle the overlapping responsibilities between the federal and the provincial levels because of the lack of coordination, this project of establishing a department of federal-provincial affairs would provide a way to find the required solutions in the best interest of the federal and provincial governments.
As a Quebec representative in this house, I know how often our province and its


people were unfairly treated1 by Liberal administrations during 22 years and afterwards by Conservative administrations because they said that Quebec was a province like the other provinces. Quebec is not a province like the other provinces. It is different from the others in many ways and particularly in its character, its French speaking population, its education system, its religious institutions, its social organization, the philosophy and habits of its people, etc., all of which is the heritage of 355 years of French Canadian history.
It is abnormal, for instance, for the federal government to impinge upon the rights of the provinces, and that is why the equalization system which was advocated by the Liberal party is not the answer to the fiscal problem of the provinces. If the provinces have the rights to which they are entitled, there is no need for them to have an equalization system.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) said a few moments ago that if that department were established, it would in effect destroy any good relationship between the federal and provincial health departments. That is not the purpose of this proposal.
He also said that the federal government gave back to the province of Alberta 44 per cent of the levies. I would point out to the hon. member that that money had been first levied by the federal government whereas it belonged to the province.
Far from wanting to promote federal interference in provincial affairs, this motion has been introduced for the purpose of settling the matter.
